chapter.title: Meet the builder: the terminal and your first request

cards.body:
Once Claude Code is installed, your first working program is about three lines away: two short commands and one plain-English sentence.

Think of Claude Code as a builder you've hired. **The builder works on whatever plot you walk it to**, and that plot is a folder on your computer. You pick the site and name the job, then you go and look at what's standing there.
cards.simpler: Once Claude Code is installed, your first working program is about three lines away: two short commands and one sentence in plain English. Picture Claude Code as a builder you've hired. **The builder works on whatever plot you walk it to**, and that plot is a folder on your computer. You choose the spot and say what to build. Then you go and look at what got built.

cards.prompt: Your terminal is sitting in a folder called birthday-card. You start Claude Code and ask for a page that says 'Happy 40th, Dev'. Where does the new file land?

options.text: In a hidden Claude folder somewhere online
In birthday-card, the folder you started it in
On your Desktop, where new files usually go

whyNot.a: That's the chat website, not Claude Code: Claude Code writes real files on your own computer.
whyNot.c: That's where screenshots often land, not where the builder works: it builds in the folder you started it in.

cards.reteach: Claude Code doesn't choose a spot. It builds right where you were standing when you started it. A builder works on the plot you drove them to, not the one next door.

cards.title: The terminal is the site gate
cards.body:
The *terminal* is a plain text window where you type commands instead of clicking. On a Mac it's the app called Terminal. On Windows it's PowerShell. It looks like 1985. That's fine.

**A terminal is always standing in one folder.** You move around with cd, short for *change directory* (directory is the old word for folder). Typing cd Desktop/first-app walks you there. On some Windows PCs, OneDrive keeps the Desktop in a different place, so that path may need adjusting.

Now type claude and press Enter. The builder starts in that exact spot and waits for your request in normal English. The first time only, install it with the one-line command on Anthropic's Claude Code page, sign in, and say yes when it asks whether you trust the folder.
cards.simpler: The terminal is a plain text window where you type commands instead of clicking. On a Mac it's Terminal. On Windows it's PowerShell. It looks old. That's fine. **A terminal always stands in one folder.** Type cd Desktop/first-app to walk there (cd means change directory, an old word for folder). On some Windows PCs, OneDrive moves the Desktop, so the path may differ. Then type claude and press Enter. The builder starts there, waiting for your request in plain English. The first time, install it from Anthropic's Claude Code page, sign in, and say yes when it asks if you trust the folder.

cards.title: Priya feeds a cat that doesn't exist
cards.body: Priya makes a folder called first-app on her Desktop, types cd Desktop/first-app, then claude. Her request: 'Make one web page called index.html with a big button that says Feed the cat, and a number that goes up by 1 each click.' Claude explains what it plans to make and asks permission to create the file, and she picks Yes. She double-clicks index.html, it opens in her browser, and she clicks 14 times. **One sentence in, one working page out**, and a cat that has now been fed 14 times without ever existing.
cards.simpler: Priya makes a first-app folder on her Desktop, types cd Desktop/first-app, then claude. She asks for one web page called index.html with a big Feed the cat button and a number that goes up by 1 each click. Claude says what it plans and asks to create the file. She picks Yes. She double-clicks index.html, it opens in her browser, and she clicks 14 times. **One sentence in, one working page out.** A made-up cat, fed 14 times.

cards.prompt: Marco wants a tip calculator inside a folder called tips on his Desktop. He has just opened a fresh terminal. Which order gets the builder to the right site?

options.text: Type claude straight away, then ask for the tip calculator
Type cd Desktop/tips, then claude, then ask for one bill-splitting page
Type the request first, then type claude

whyNot.a: That's starting the builder before walking to the site: a fresh terminal usually starts in your home folder, so the file lands there.
whyNot.c: That's the request before the builder: the terminal doesn't understand English until claude is running.

cards.reteach: The order is walk, then start, then ask. cd takes you to the folder, claude starts the builder there, and only then does your plain-English request go in.

cards.title: Ask for something you can see
cards.body:
You'd think your first request should be impressive. It's the opposite: **make the first job tiny and visible**, like one page with one button, something you can open and poke in 10 seconds. If it works, you know every link works: terminal, folder, builder, file.

Before Claude creates or changes a file, it shows you what it's about to do and asks. That's you holding the keys. Read what it plans, then say yes.

When it's done, go and look. Open the folder in Finder or File Explorer and double-click the file. A .html file opens in your web browser with no extra setup.
cards.simpler: Your first request shouldn't be impressive. **Make the first job tiny and visible**: one page, one button, something you can open and try in 10 seconds. If it works, every link works: terminal, folder, builder, file. Before Claude creates or changes a file, it shows its plan and asks. You hold the keys, so read it, then say yes. Then open the folder in Finder or File Explorer and double-click the file. A .html file opens straight in your browser.

cards.body: Sam opens Terminal, types claude, and asks for a recipe page. It works, but he can't find the file. A fresh terminal usually starts in your *home folder*, so his page is sitting between Downloads and Music. To catch this before you start, type pwd (short for print working directory) and the terminal names the folder you're in. **If it isn't your project folder, cd there first.**
cards.simpler: Sam opens Terminal, types claude, and asks for a recipe page. It works, but he can't find the file. A new terminal usually starts in your home folder, the main folder for your account, so his page landed next to Downloads and Music. To catch this first, type pwd (short for print working directory) and the terminal tells you which folder you're in. **If it isn't your project folder, cd there first.**

cards.prompt: Aisha asked for a quiz page and Claude said it made quiz.html. Her quiz folder is still empty. What most likely happened?

options.text: Claude only pretended and made nothing
She started Claude while standing in a different folder
HTML files stay hidden until you put them online

whyNot.a: That's mixing up a missing file with a fake one: the file most likely exists, just in whatever folder she was standing in when she typed claude.
whyNot.c: That's mixing up saving with going live: a .html file sits in its folder like any other file, no publishing needed.

cards.reteach: The builder always works on the site you walked it to. If a file is missing from the folder you expected, check where you were when you typed claude. pwd will tell you. Then cd to the right folder and start again.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body:
Claude Code is a builder that works in **whichever folder your terminal is standing in**, so you cd to your project folder, type claude, and ask in plain English. Start with one tiny thing you can see, approve the file, then go and check it's really there.

Picture it as walking the builder to an empty plot, pointing at the ground, saying 'one shed, please', then coming back to knock on the door.
cards.simpler: Claude Code is a builder that works in **whichever folder your terminal is standing in**. So cd to your project folder, type claude, and ask in plain English. Start with one tiny thing you can see. Approve the file, then go check that it's really there. Picture walking the builder to an empty plot, pointing, saying 'one shed, please', then coming back to knock on the door.

cards.body:
Make a folder called coffee on your Desktop. Walk your terminal there, start claude, and ask for one page with a button that counts your coffees today, plus a short warning that shows up after the third one. Approve the file, open it, and log today's coffees honestly.

Tomorrow: why 'make it better' is the worst thing you can say to a builder.
cards.simpler:
Make a folder called coffee on your Desktop. Use cd to walk the terminal there, then type claude. Ask for **one page with a button that counts your coffees today**, and a short warning after the third one. When Claude asks to create the file, say yes. Then open the page and log today's coffees.

Tomorrow: why 'make it better' is the worst thing you can say to a builder.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now start Claude Code inside a folder, ask for one small thing in plain English, and open the file it made.

dubious_claims: 'three lines away' skips the first-time install, sign-in, and the 'do you trust this folder' prompt, so the real first run is more than three lines
'cd Desktop/first-app' in a fresh PowerShell can fail on Windows machines where OneDrive moves the Desktop to a different folder
Card 8 feedback says 'she approved a real file', but the exercise never says she approved anything
repairedFrom.why: The try card repeats Priya's example almost word for word (same folder, same counter button, same 14 clicks), so it asks for no new thinking. It also comes after the 'Tomorrow' line, so the chapter ends on 'click 14 times' instead of the hook for the next chapter. Other failures: the 'In one breath' teach card has no concrete image. Card 8's feedback says 'wrong address', and 'blaming the builder' doesn't name what the reader mixed up. All three exercises test the same easy point, so a reader who isn't already interested may get bored before the end.
repairedFrom.fix: Rewrite the try as the reader's own small build (e.g. 'a page with a button that counts your coffees today, in a folder called coffee'), then move 'Tomorrow: why make it better is the worst thing you can say to a builder' to be its final line.
